extracted.intended_audience: law students, judges, and legal practitioners interested in foundations and interpretation of municipal law
extracted.subtask_description: Explicating what constitutes municipal law and how to interpret and apply it (Blackstone's account): definitions, parts of law, promulgation, retrospective laws, obligations, interpretation signs, equity, and distinctions between unwritten and written law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law as a rule (distinct from advice and compact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal law is defined as 'a rule' (a rule of civil conduct) and is distinguished from advice or counsel and from a compact or agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law differs from counsel because counsel is persuasion (follow or not), while law depends on the maker's will and acts upon the unwilling as well as the willing. A compact proceeds from us (promise: 'I will or will not'), whereas law is a command directed to us ('thou shalt or shalt not'). Although a compact carries a conscientious obligation, its original source of obligation differs from that of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal law as a rule of civil conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal law is 'a rule of civil conduct' distinguishing it from natural or revealed law which govern moral conduct (and faith in the revealed case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal/civil law regards individuals as citizens with duties arising from membership in the common union — duties to contribute to the subsistence and peace of society, beyond mere natural or religious duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promulgation requirement ('prescribed')
rubrics_metrics.description: A law must be 'prescribed'—the legislator's resolution must be notified to the people who are to obey it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promulgation may occur by universal tradition/long practice (common law), viva voce by officers (proclamations), or by writing/printing (statutes). Whatever the mode, promulgators must notify laws in the most public and perspicuous manner. Anti-patterns: secretive or obscure promulgation (e.g., Caligula's tiny script) and making laws ex post facto (declaring an act criminal only after it was committed) are unjust. All laws should commence in futuro and be notified before commencement; subjects are expected to acquaint themselves with promulgated laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ex post facto laws; laws should operate prospectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Making laws 'ex post facto' (declaring an action criminal after it was committed) is unreasonable and unjust because the party could not foresee the law and had no cause to abstain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such laws are cruel and unjust; laws should commence in futuro and be notified before commencement. Failure to notify removes the foundation for legal obligation and renders punishment unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawmaking by the supreme power (sovereignty requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal law must be 'prescribed by the supreme power in a state' — it is requisite to the essence of a law that it be made by the supreme authority (sovereignty/legislature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever the sovereign power resides, that authority has the right (and duty) to make laws; other state powers must conform to and be directed by the legislative power. Sovereignty implies both the right and the duty to prescribe rules of civil action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations of society and implied original contract
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural foundations of society are the wants and fears of individuals; association implies an original (often implied) contract that the whole will protect its parts and each part will pay obedience to the will of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone rejects the literal historic state-of-nature story as improbable but recognizes an implied political union: individuals submit private wills to a collective will to obtain protection. This theoretical original contract explains why laws and government arise and why individuals owe obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities requisite in sovereigns/government
rubrics_metrics.description: Good government should be reposed in persons possessing wisdom, goodness, and power (strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wisdom discerns the community's real interest; goodness pursues that interest; and strength executes it. These three are the natural foundations of sovereignty and should be found in any well-constituted government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of forms of government by their chief virtues and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical three forms—democracy (sovereign in the people), aristocracy (council of select members), monarchy (single person)—each have characteristic advantages and disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracies tend toward public virtue but may be foolish and weak in execution; aristocracies supply wisdom but less honesty and strength; monarchies supply strength and dispatch but risk improvidence or oppression. Mixed constitutions (combining features) attempt to reconcile these qualities (example: British constitution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and duty of legislation (right and duty to make laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since members of a community are bound to conform to the will of the state, it is expedient and the duty of the supreme power to issue general rules for the perpetual information and direction of all persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation defines what is one's own and another's, absolute and relative duties, what is honest or dishonest, and what liberties individuals retain after joining society; laws provide uniform rules so the community can act as one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of a law: declaratory, directory, remedial, sanction/vindicatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Every law consists of parts: (1) declaratory—defines rights and wrongs; (2) directory—enjoins observance of rights and forbids wrongs; (3) remedial—provides methods to recover rights or redress wrongs; (4) sanction/vindicatory—specifies penalties for public wrongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory part often transcribes natural/divine principles for crimes mala in se but has special force when creating duties or offences that are indifferent in nature. Directory and declaratory are interrelated. Remedial provisions are essential to make declarations meaningful (example: possession restored and damages). Sanctions are generally punitive (vindicatory) rather than remuneratory; the penalty annexed is the main strength of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of declaratory law vis-à-vis natural rights and positive duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Declaratory law adds no additional force to natural rights (life, liberty) and cannot abridge them; but it can create rights/wrongs for things indifferent in themselves to promote societal welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human legislature acts subordinate to superior laws in declaring natural rights; yet for mala prohibita (positive duties), municipal law determines what is right or wrong. Examples: marital property rules and statutes against monopolies are creations of municipal law, not natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of sanctions (penalties) in producing obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: The main strength and force of a law consists in the penalty annexed to it; obligation arises not from natural compulsion but from the declared punishment which makes disobedience undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While rewards may persuade, punishment is the truly compulsory element. Legislators therefore typically make sanctions vindicatory rather than remuneratory. Regulators should note that the dread of evil commonly motivates conduct more than prospect of reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience and the binding force of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Human laws are binding on men's consciences regarding rights and natural duties; but in positive-law offences (mala prohibita), conscience obliges only to submit to the penalty if incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rights determined by law and for mala in se offences, conscience aligns with law because of superior moral law. For mere penal statutes that prohibit otherwise indifferent acts, the transgression is not necessarily a moral or conscientious wrong—only the payment of the penalty is morally required once adjudicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper methods of legal interpretation (signs of legislator's intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain the legislator's intention at the time the law was made, one should use the most natural and probable signs: words, context, subject matter, effects and consequence, and the spirit and reason of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Words: use usual/popular meaning; technical terms take technical sense; when words are repugnant between laws, the later law prevails (leges posteriores...). 2) Context: compare ambiguous words with preamble and related statutes or laws by same legislator. 3) Subject matter: read words in light of the law's object (example: 'provisions' meant appointments, not grain). 4) Effects/consequences: avoid literal meaning when it leads to absurdity (example: surgeon drawing blood). 5) Spirit/reason: give weight to the law's purpose; when reason ceases, law should cease. These signs are preferred over interrogating the legislature for particular decisions (rescripts), which is criticized as a bad method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: reliance on rescripts or particular answers from legislature for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting particular disputes to the legislature (e.g., emperor's rescripts) is a poor method of interpretation because it is endless and invites partiality and oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescripts may gain force by repetition but ought to be distinguished from general constitutions. Judicial interpreters should prefer construction by signs (words, context, subject matter, effects, reason) rather than depending on ad hoc executive answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reason and spirit of law gives rise to equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting laws by their reason and spirit yields equity: the correction of what the law (by reason of universality) is deficient in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity allows exception of circumstances the legislator would have excepted had they been foreseen ('lex non exacte definit, sed arbitrio boni viri permittit'). But equity cannot be reduced to fixed rules without destroying its essence; excessive indulgence of equitable discretion risks turning judges into legislators and producing confusion. Balance: law without equity is harsh but preferable to equity without law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between lex non scripta (unwritten/common law) and lex scripta (written/statute law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal law of England divides into lex non scripta (unwritten/common law, including general customs, particular customs, and customs of particular courts) and lex scripta (written/statute law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unwritten laws today have their monuments in court records, reports, and learned treatises; they are called 'non scripta' because their origin is not set down in legislative acts but they bind by long immemorial usage and universal reception. Examples: ancient British and Gallic customary retention, records preserved in courts and reports.
